That "problem" is a myth in and of itself.

A) There are no "terminal" (the proper term for non-reproductive crops) GMO crops put out on the market

B) The farmer keeping a portion of his harvest to use next spring as seed is a romanticized portrait that died out with the advent of modern agriculture. It's pretty much always cheaper to sell your product on the market and buy seeds from a dedicated company. (There's a reason we don't knit our own clothing at home these days either.)

C) Of the GMO crops on the market by far the most common are "roundup ready" varieties. Roundup is the marketing name for a herbicide containing Glyphosate as the active ingredient, glyphosate interferes with protein synthesis in most species of plants preventing them from growing. The modification was the gene for glyphosate immunity was transplanted into the crop species, thus when you spray roundup it doesn't impact your crops but weeds can't grow. The second major GMO product on the market produces a pesticide derived from a bacteria that's toxic to insects but harmless to mammals. The advantage to having it hardwritten into the plant's DNA as opposed to sprayed on is that you only end up killing target insects feeding on your crops rather than killing off non-target species, as well as not having to reapply it regularly when it gets washed off in the rain.

As to why Farmers use them? Because it makes sense. You get more yield from less land, putting less labor into weed/pest control. Anti-GMO folks will point out that there wasn't a huge productivity spike, but the real takeaway is that we've maintained productivity while dramatically scaling back on labor, land impact, and resource use. No till farming made viable by glyphosate as an example maintains soil integrity much better, reduces water consumption, and reduces the need for fertilizer as the nutrients don't get "washed out" of the tilled soil.
